subtype: Approach: going through a mutual connection [Action]
passage: Keerthana, you asked how I got the reply from the analyst. Honestly I had written to her cold two weeks before and heard nothing. Then in a lecture, Prof. Menon mentioned a former student who now works in the same team. Something clicked. After class I asked, "Ma'am, is it the same person? Would you be comfortable introducing me? Just one line, please." She smiled, said "Send me two lines about what you want," and I did. That evening she forwarded my note with a friendly message on top. The analyst replied in a day, "Any friend of Prof. Menon's, happy to talk." I'm Anjali, and I have learned that a warm door beats a cold email.

qa.q: What did Prof. Menon ask Anjali to send?
qa.a: Prof. Menon asked Anjali to send two lines about what Anjali wanted.

qa.q: What was Anjali feeling after two weeks of silence from the analyst?
qa.a: Anjali was disappointed and a little discouraged, until the lecture comment made something click.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Anjali use if the professor could not help, and why?
qa.a: Anjali could look for a shared club or former classmate who knows the analyst, because any mutual contact can make the first contact warmer.

qa.q: How might Prof. Menon see the request?
qa.a: Prof. Menon is asked politely for a one-line introduction, gets two lines about the goal and forwards it, so the professor probably sees a student who is easy to help.

grounding: Shows using a mutual contact, a professor, for an introduction that earns a warmer reply than a cold message.

subtype: Approach: going through a mutual connection [Action]
passage:
I'm Avni, Darshan's lab partner, and I was there when he stopped cold-messaging people. For a month he had been sending short notes to a marine researcher in Goa, Dr Farah Siddiqui, about her coral work. Two notes, no reply.
Then, in our lab, he noticed a group photo on Professor Joshi's wall: our professor and Dr Siddiqui at a conference, laughing. Darshan stared at it for a while. Next day he waited after class and asked Professor Joshi, a bit awkwardly, whether he knew her well enough to introduce him in one line.
The professor wrote the email right there, copying Darshan in: 'Farah, a sharp student of mine is keen on reef monitoring. Would you give him fifteen minutes?'
Dr Siddiqui replied that evening, warmly, with three possible times. I saw Darshan read it twice. I can't say what he felt, but he grinned through the whole practical.

qa.q: What did Darshan notice on Professor Joshi's wall?
qa.a: A group photo of the professor and Dr Siddiqui at a conference, laughing.

qa.q: What might Darshan have felt when asking Professor Joshi for the introduction?
qa.a: He likely felt awkward and nervous about asking a favour, but hopeful, since the photo showed a real link.

qa.q: What should Darshan do before the fifteen-minute call?
qa.a: Thank Professor Joshi, read Dr Siddiqui's recent coral work, and prepare two specific questions so the warm introduction is used well.

qa.q: How does the introduction look to Dr Siddiqui?
qa.a: It comes from a colleague she knows, so a student she had not answered now feels worth a warm, quick reply.

grounding: Shows a student learning that a professor knows a target researcher, asking for a short introduction, and getting a warmer reply than cold notes did.

subtype: Approach: going through a mutual connection [Action]
passage:
Monday. Manoj has written twice to Vikas Rao, who runs a small robotics startup in Coimbatore. No reply either time. In the lab, his guide, Professor Anand, mentions that Vikas was once her student.
Wednesday. Manoj waits outside her cabin after the lab session, practising the sentence. 'Ma'am, would you be comfortable introducing me to Vikas Rao? Just two lines. I want to ask about their gripper design.' She thinks, nods, and says she will send it once she has read his project report.
Friday. The email goes out: 'Vikas, Manoj is working on low-cost grippers in my lab. He has a good question for you. Could you find fifteen minutes?' Within two hours Vikas replies to both: 'Of course, for your students always. Manoj, how about Monday at six?' Manoj forwards the reply to his mother with one word: 'Monday!'

qa.q: What is Manoj working on, according to the professor's email?
qa.a: Low-cost grippers, in the professor's lab.

qa.q: How was Manoj likely feeling on Wednesday while waiting outside the cabin?
qa.a: He was probably nervous about asking a favour, which is why he kept practising the sentence.

qa.q: What could Manoj do after the call to keep the connection warm?
qa.a: Thank both Vikas and Professor Anand, and later share how the gripper advice changed the project.

qa.q: How might Vikas see the email from Professor Anand?
qa.a: It comes from a former teacher, so it feels like a trusted request rather than a stranger's note, and Vikas replies within two hours.

grounding: Shows a student asking a professor who knows the target person for a short introduction, which gets a quick, warm reply after cold notes failed.
